title: Kenyan Tamarind Juice
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: Kenyan Tamarind Juice — tangy, sweet-sour tamarind pulp dissolved in water with sugar and a pinch of salt. One of the most refreshing drinks of the Kenyan coast — deeply flavourful, uniquely tart, and beautifully cooling on a hot coastal day.
longDesc: Tamarind juice has been a staple refreshment of the Kenyan coast for centuries — the fruit brought through Indian Ocean trade routes that planted tamarind trees along the entire East African coastline. The juice, strained from soaked tamarind pulp and balanced with sugar and salt, has a complex sweet-sour-fruity character unlike any other juice. Chilled and served over ice, it is extraordinarily refreshing.
ingredients: 4 cups cold water — plus hot water for soaking
¼ tsp ground cumin — optional, for depth

substitutions.alternative: 4 tbsp tamarind paste dissolved in 4 cups water

steps: Break the tamarind block into pieces. Place in a bowl with 2 cups of hot water.
Soak for 15 minutes. Use your hands to squeeze and break down the pulp, releasing the juice.
Strain through a fine mesh strainer, pressing to extract all the juice. Discard the fibres and seeds.
Add the remaining 2 cups of cold water to the strained tamarind liquid.
Add sugar and salt. Stir until dissolved. Taste and adjust.
Add cumin if using — it adds a subtle warmth.
Chill or serve immediately over ice.
chefTips: The balance of sweet and sour is personal — start with 4 tbsp sugar and adjust.
A pinch of salt sharpens all the flavours dramatically — do not skip it.
Ground cumin, while optional, gives the juice a subtle roasted depth that makes it more interesting.
commonMistakes: Not straining thoroughly — fibrous, grainy juice.
Too much water — dilutes the distinctive tamarind character.

faqs.q: Can I use ready-made tamarind paste?
faqs.a: Yes — dissolve 4 tbsp of tamarind paste in 4 cups of water. Adjust sugar and salt to taste.

cookingScience: Tamarind contains tartaric acid, malic acid, and citric acid — a complex combination that gives it a more layered sourness than lemon (only citric acid). The salt enhances sweetness perception through sodium-ion interaction with taste receptors, which is why salted tamarind juice tastes sweeter and more rounded than unsalted.
sustainabilityTips: Tamarind trees are perennial and drought-tolerant — one of the most sustainable fruit trees on the Kenyan coast.
healthBenefits: Tamarind is rich in tartaric acid, B vitamins, and iron.
culturalNote: Tamarind juice is one of the oldest refreshments of the Kenyan coast — sold by vendors along the beach and at coastal markets, it has been quenching the thirst of traders, travellers, and residents for centuries.
regionalVariations: Spiced tamarind with cumin and black salt.
